claims.text: Wear performance in HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation activity.
Impeded dislocation activity reduces plastic deformation under frictional stress.
Impeded dislocation activity reduces crack initiation under frictional stress.
The proposed baseline is an equiatomic, nominally quinary HEA coating produced by sputter deposition and annealing.
The baseline should contain minimal secondary phases or grain-boundary precipitates.
Adding 2–5 at.% Hf or Nb will increase local lattice distortion.
The wear comparison will use identical processing, substrate, counterface, and surface-finish conditions apart from doping.
The hypothesis is to be tested under dry sliding or pin-on-disk wear at ambient temperature and loads up to approximately 80 N.
Changes associated with local lattice distortion can be tracked using X-ray or neutron diffraction and electron microscopy.
Doping-induced lattice distortion elevates local strain fields.
The elevated strain fields hinder dislocation movement.
Hindered dislocation movement reduces crack nucleation and material removal during sliding.
Doped coatings should have a wear rate approximately 20–40% lower than the undoped baseline.
Doped coatings should exhibit a lower friction coefficient than the undoped baseline.
The proposed effect should hold below major phase-transformation temperatures and at loads where plastic deformation contributes to wear.
Very high temperatures, severe oxidation, or a change in wear mode may invalidate the proposed effect.
The magnitude of wear improvement may depend on processing history and dopant identity.
Secondary-phase formation may overshadow the effect attributed to lattice distortion.
Failure of wear rate to improve with measured increases in lattice distortion, or worsening wear with increased distortion, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
